picks.title: 95 - What is Suffering (Dukkha) in Buddhism
picks.summary: Why do we suffer? Why does life feel painful, stressful, or disappointing even when things seem to be going well? In this episode, we explore suffering from a practical Buddhist perspective not as a concept, but as a lived human experience. Sometimes referred to as 'suffering' in the West, 'Dukkha' has a much deeper range and significance. Drawing from the Buddha’s core insights into impermanence, dependent origination, the Three Poisons/Fires, karma, and rebirth, we look at how suffering arises, why we add extra layers of pain through craving and clinging, and what the Buddhist path offers as
picks.reason: A clear, practical exploration of suffering (dukkha) from core Buddhist teachings.

picks.title: Tim Geil: Exploring Anatta: Non-Self
picks.summary: (Cambridge Insight Meditation Center) Anatta, or non-self, is a core teaching of the Buddha, and yet can be confusing and bewildering. Sometimes the sense of self loves trying to get rid of itself, all the while maintaining itself on subtle levels. Yet, anatta is our true nature, and we release and relax into non-separation and unity. Qualities of compassion and the heart often support this understanding more than our intellect. This talk will explore anatta from a practical and experiential perspective.
picks.reason: Deep exploration of the core Buddhist teaching of non-self (anatta).

picks.title: How They Meditate – Ajahn Brahm (Guided Meditation)
picks.summary:
This is part of our series How They Meditate, covering various meditation teachers and their styles. Visit https://OneMindDharma.com/howtheymeditate to see all episodes.



Ajahn Brahm is a senior Thai Forest monk, although his monastery was stripped of its status as an official Thai Forest monastery. We discuss that more in this episode.



His teachings center on his idea of the “beautiful breath.” Unlike the first three episodes of the series, Ajahn Brahm focuses on jhana, or states of deep concentration. His teaching style is humorous, light-hearted, and centers on letting go.

picks.title: Sense Restraint | Self Control | Indriya Samvara | AN Eights #9 'Nanda Sutta'| Ajahn Dhammasiha
picks.summary: The Buddha's half-brother Venerable Nanda was the foremost bhikkhu disciple in terms of sense restraint. He was attractive, handsome, strong and had a natural inclination to intense sensual desire, which caused him major struggles in the beginning of his monk's life. He overcame his difficulties through: Sense Restraint (Indriya Saṃvara) Knowing the right amount when eating (Bhojanasmiṃ Mattaññutā) Dedication to Wakefulness (Jāgariyaṃ Anuyutta) Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension (Sati Sampajañña)Anguttara Nikāya / Numerical Discourse, Eights, No 9 'Nanda Sutta' See also: Saṃyutta Nikāya / Col
picks.reason: Teaching on sense restraint and self-control from the Nanda Sutta in Buddhist monastic context.

picks.title: 341 - Five Kinds of Appropriate Longing (2 of 2)
picks.summary: Many people think that the aim of Buddhism is let go of any kind of longing. However, without wholesome desires – to awaken, to act ethically, to honor your relationships, etc. – you wouldn't progress in practice. In Part 1 I started discussing five kinds of appropriate longing based loosely on the Vajrayana teaching of the five wisdom energies, covering Red and Yellow energy longing. In Part 2, I talk about Blue, Green, and White energy.
picks.reason: Examines wholesome longing and desire as part of Buddhist spiritual progress.

picks.title: Being real
picks.summary:
In this Wednesday Night Dharma Talk, Frank Ostaseski traces what he learned sitting at the bedside of thousands of dying people: “to sit next to people and not mess with them. Not try and help them have some experience, or meet someone else’s agenda, including their own. Just sit with them.” That same quality of presence, he suggests, is what it means to ‘be real’ — an alignment with reality…
Source
picks.reason: Shares lessons on presence and being real from sitting with the dying.

picks.showTitle: Zen Stories & Buddhist Teachings for Sleep by Midnight Monk
picks.title: Let People Be Who They Are - Fall Asleep to Buddhist Teachings & Zen Stories for Peace & Letting Go
picks.summary: Tonight we explore what the Buddha and the Zen masters understood about the people closest to us, and why the ones we love are so often the ones we find hardest to accept. Through calm Buddhist stories and Zen teachings for sleep, we look at judgment, blame, and the wish for others to change, and discover the freedom that comes from letting people be who they are.This episode draws on more than two thousand years of Buddhist wisdom: teachings on compassion, mindful listening, right speech, acceptance, and the deep connection between us that judgment hides from view. It is a long, slow journey
picks.reason: Buddhist stories and teachings on acceptance and compassion toward others.
